questions.question: A stable patient has regular narrow-complex tachycardia with RP longer than PR and negative P waves in the inferior leads. Adenosine terminates the episode. Which conclusion is most defensible from these findings alone?
options: Negative inferior P waves establish permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia
Adenosine termination establishes atypical AVNRT
Atypical AVNRT, slowly conducting-pathway AVRT and adenosine-sensitive atrial tachycardia remain possible
RP longer than PR establishes focal atrial tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Long-RP Supraventricular Tachycardia

Correct answer: Atypical AVNRT, slowly conducting-pathway AVRT and adenosine-sensitive atrial tachycardia remain possible

Long-RP Differential

**RP longer than PR describes timing, not a unique mechanism.**

Consider atypical AVNRT, slowly conducting orthodromic AVRT such as PJRT, and focal atrial tachycardia.

Interpret Adenosine Carefully

**Termination does not prove one circuit.**

AV-node-dependent reentry may stop, but some focal atrial tachycardias are also adenosine-sensitive.

**Inspect atrial activity during AV block and termination.**

Negative inferior P waves suggest activation direction, not definitive circuit anatomy; recurrent or unclear episodes may require EPS.

Mechanism | Reason for long RP | Important qualification

Atypical AVNRT | Delayed retrograde nodal activation | Inferiorly negative P waves can resemble PJRT

PJRT | Slow decremental retrograde accessory pathway | No baseline delta wave is required

Focal AT | Atrial focus with its own activation timing | Some forms terminate with adenosine

Negative inferior P waves establish permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia: PJRT often has long RP and inferiorly negative retrograde P waves, but atypical AVNRT and low atrial foci can resemble this pattern. Additional electrophysiological evidence is needed before assigning that specific pathway mechanism.

Adenosine termination establishes atypical AVNRT: Atypical AVNRT can terminate with adenosine, but slowly conducting accessory-pathway AVRT and some focal AT mechanisms can do so as well. The drug response is not a unique circuit identifier.

RP longer than PR establishes focal atrial tachycardia: Focal AT is an important long-RP diagnosis, but delayed retrograde conduction during atypical AVNRT or AVRT can produce the same surface timing relationship. RP classification narrows rather than completes the differential.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: During a regular narrow-complex tachycardia, adenosine causes several nonconducted atrial impulses. Discrete abnormal P waves continue at the same cycle length, separated by an isoelectric baseline, and one-to-one ventricular conduction then resumes. Which interpretation best fits the observed response?
options: An atrial tachycardia continuing independently of transient AV nodal block
Orthodromic AVRT continuing through the blocked AV node
Sinus tachycardia established by adenosine resistance
Typical AVNRT established by resumption of one-to-one conduction
questions.explanation:
Adenosine Unmasks Continuing Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: An atrial tachycardia continuing independently of transient AV nodal block

Continuing Atrial Activity

**Transient AV block exposes an atrial rhythm that continues at its original cycle length.**

Discrete abnormal P waves separated by an isoelectric baseline support atrial tachycardia.

What the Response Establishes

**Ordinary orthodromic AVRT requires AV nodal antegrade conduction**, so blocking that limb usually terminates the circuit.

**Adenosine slowing is not synonymous with conversion.**

Record the atria throughout the maneuver; AVNRT can occasionally continue despite block below its circuit, so use the full atrial pattern rather than AV block alone.

Orthodromic AVRT continuing through the blocked AV node: The AV node is the antegrade limb of ordinary orthodromic AVRT. Sustained atrial activity at an unchanged cycle despite interruption of that limb argues against this circuit as the explanation.

Sinus tachycardia established by adenosine resistance: Sinus activity can continue during transient AV block, but adenosine resistance does not establish sinus origin. The abnormal discrete P-wave morphology supports a non-sinus atrial source in this recording.

Typical AVNRT established by resumption of one-to-one conduction: AVNRT can rarely continue with block below its circuit, so absent ventricular responses alone do not settle every case. Here the independently continuing discrete abnormal atrial rhythm favors AT, and resumption of conduction is not proof of nodal reentry.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A patient has repeated narrow-complex tachycardia at 140–160/min. Each episode has one consistent P-wave morphology different from sinus rhythm, with an isoelectric interval between P waves. The atrial rate gradually accelerates at onset, and occasional AV block occurs without changing atrial timing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Focal Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: Focal atrial tachycardia

Focal Atrial Tachycardia

**A consistent non-sinus P morphology with discrete atrial waves supports a focal source.**

Warm-up/cool-down suggests abnormal automaticity; some focal AT uses triggered activity or localized reentry.

Assess Consequences

**Persistence through AV block supports an atrial driver.**

The ventricular response can vary without changing the atrial cycle.

**Incessant AT can cause tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.**

Assess burden, LV function and reversible triggers; recurrent symptomatic or incessant disease merits specialist treatment, often including ablation assessment.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia: MAT has changing P-wave morphologies and irregular atrial timing. A single reproducible non-sinus morphology with an organized atrial cycle instead supports a single dominant atrial activation source.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: Typical AVNRT usually has abrupt onset and near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation. Persistent independent abnormal atrial activity and warm-up favor an atrial source rather than that usual nodal circuit.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs AV conduction as part of its circuit. Continued atrial tachycardia through AV block, together with non-sinus P waves and gradual acceleration, supports a focal atrial mechanism.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: During an exacerbation of COPD, a patient has an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 125/min. A single lead shows at least three distinct P-wave morphologies, variable P–P and PR intervals, and isoelectric segments between atrial deflections. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Atrial fibrillation
Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction
Sinus tachycardia with frequent atrial premature beats
questions.explanation:
Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: Multifocal atrial tachycardia

MAT Criteria

**Irregular atrial rhythm >100/min with ≥3 P-wave morphologies in one lead.**

PP, PR and RR vary; an isoelectric baseline separates P waves. A slower counterpart is wandering atrial pacemaker.

Management

**Treat pulmonary/systemic illness and correct potassium/magnesium.**

Hypoxemia, severe COPD, adrenergic stress and contributing drugs are common contexts.

**Do not label it AF merely because RR is irregular.**

Discrete varying P waves distinguish MAT; cardioversion is usually ineffective, and anticoagulation is not prescribed solely for MAT.

Rhythm | Atrial finding | Timing clue

MAT | At least 3 discrete P morphologies in one lead | Irregular P–P; rate >100/min

Wandering atrial pacemaker | Multiple discrete P morphologies | Similar pattern at a slower rate

AF | No consistent discrete P sequence | Irregular ventricular response unless another mechanism intervenes

Flutter with variable block | Repeating organized atrial activation | Irregular ventricular conduction with organized atrial cycle

Atrial fibrillation: AF has disorganized atrial activation without consistently identifiable discrete P waves. Irregularity alone is insufficient: the multiple discrete P morphologies and intervening isoelectric baseline support MAT.

Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction: Variable conduction can make flutter ventricular intervals irregular, but the underlying atrial cycle is usually organized and repetitive. Changing P-wave morphologies and irregular atrial intervals favor MAT.

Sinus tachycardia with frequent atrial premature beats: Sinus rhythm with ectopy retains a dominant sinus sequence interrupted by premature beats. A sustained irregular atrial rhythm with several recurring morphologies and no dominant sinus cycle is more consistent with MAT.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia runs at 150/min. During a monitored diagnostic maneuver, ventricular conduction briefly slows and continuous atrial activity at 300/min becomes visible, with repetitive negative deflections in the inferior leads. Which diagnosis best explains the original rhythm?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia with one-to-one conduction
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Atrial flutter with two-to-one AV conduction
questions.explanation:
Atrial Flutter With Concealed Two-to-One Conduction

Correct answer: Atrial flutter with two-to-one AV conduction

Flutter With 2:1 Conduction

**Atrial activity near 300/min can produce a ventricular rate near 150/min.**

Alternate flutter waves may be hidden in QRS/T waves; 150/min is a clue, not a diagnostic threshold.

Unmask the Atria

**Transient AV nodal slowing reveals continuing macroreentry.**

Typical counterclockwise CTI-dependent flutter often has negative inferior waves and positive V1 activity.

**Ventricular slowing is not necessarily termination.**

Document the atrial rhythm; assess stability, stroke prevention and rhythm strategy according to duration and clinical risk.

Focal atrial tachycardia with one-to-one conduction: Focal AT can continue through AV block, but one-to-one conduction would not explain the original atrial-to-ventricular ratio of two. Continuous repetitive flutter activity further favors macroreentry over a discrete focal P-wave pattern.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT can obscure atrial activity near the QRS, but the newly visible atrial cycle is twice the original ventricular rate and continues independently as conduction slows. This supports an atrial driver rather than ordinary one-to-one nodal reentry.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT requires atria and ventricles in its circuit. A continuing atrial rhythm at 300/min while the ventricular response slows is inconsistent with the usual one-to-one accessory-pathway circuit.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: After cardiac surgery, an adult has narrow-complex tachycardia that gradually accelerates to 135/min and later slows gradually. Sinus P waves at 85/min march independently through the rhythm, and the QRS morphology matches normally conducted baseline beats. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia with variable AV block
Orthodromic AV reentry through an accessory pathway
Typical slow–fast AV nodal reentry
Enhanced automaticity producing focal junctional tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Nonreentrant Junctional Tachycardia

Correct answer: Enhanced automaticity producing focal junctional tachycardia

Junctional Automaticity

**Gradual narrow-complex acceleration with slower independent sinus P waves supports focal junctional tachycardia.**

The AV junction activates the ventricles while atrial and ventricular timing can dissociate.

Postoperative Context

**Review catecholamines, stress, ischemia, electrolytes and drugs.**

Digoxin toxicity and postoperative tissue irritation are relevant alternative settings.

**Assess perfusion and ventricular function.**

Nonreentrant impulse formation differs from abrupt AVNRT; treatment targets triggers and rate/physiology, with specialist input when persistent or unstable.

Focal atrial tachycardia with variable AV block: Focal AT requires the rapid driver to be atrial. Here the atrial rate is slower than the ventricular rhythm and independent of it, so the atria are not supplying the tachycardic impulse sequence.

Orthodromic AV reentry through an accessory pathway: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs the atria and ventricles as circuit components. Sustained tachycardia with independent slower atrial activity argues against that mechanism rather than an accessory-pathway return limb.

Typical slow–fast AV nodal reentry: AVNRT is a reentrant mechanism, usually with abrupt onset and offset. Although rare AVNRT variants can dissociate the atria, gradual rate behavior and the postoperative context favor automatic junctional tachycardia here.

questions.question: An electrophysiology study demonstrates a regular reentrant tachycardia using antegrade conduction through the AV node and His–Purkinje system, with retrograde return through an atrioventricular accessory pathway. Which classification is correct?
options: Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Atrial tachycardia with bystander pre-excitation
questions.explanation:
Orthodromic and Antidromic AV Reentry

Correct answer: Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia

Direction of the AVRT Circuit

**Orthodromic:** AV node/His–Purkinje antegradely, accessory pathway retrogradely.

QRS is usually narrow unless aberrancy or another conduction abnormality exists.

Related Mechanisms

**Antidromic:** accessory pathway antegradely, with return through the AV node or another pathway.

Ventricular activation is pre-excited and generally wide.

**A pathway may be a bystander during AF, flutter or AVNRT.**

questions.question: A patient has recurrent abrupt regular narrow-complex tachycardia despite a normal PR interval and no delta wave on several sinus ECGs. EPS establishes an accessory pathway that conducts from ventricle to atrium but not antegradely. Which statement is correct?
options: The pathway creates the same rapid pre-excited AF mechanism as a short-refractory antegrade pathway
Absence of a delta wave makes the demonstrated pathway incapable of sustaining AVRT
The pathway can provide the antegrade limb of antidromic AVRT
The pathway can sustain orthodromic AVRT without producing resting ventricular pre-excitation
questions.explanation:
Concealed Accessory Pathways

Correct answer: The pathway can sustain orthodromic AVRT without producing resting ventricular pre-excitation

Retrograde-Only Pathway

**A concealed accessory pathway lacks antegrade conduction**, so no sinus delta wave is expected.

It can still return activation from ventricle to atrium during orthodromic AVRT.

Risk and Treatment

**A genuinely retrograde-only pathway does not transmit AF rapidly antegradely.**

This distinction concerns pathway physiology, not a declaration that all symptoms are harmless.

**Document recurrent tachycardia and assess symptom burden.**

EPS and ablation can establish and treat a symptomatic pathway; a normal resting PR/QRS does not exclude it.

The pathway creates the same rapid pre-excited AF mechanism as a short-refractory antegrade pathway: Rapid ventricular pre-excitation during AF requires antegrade accessory conduction. A truly retrograde-only pathway does not supply that mechanism, although AF and other independent risks may still occur.

Absence of a delta wave makes the demonstrated pathway incapable of sustaining AVRT: A delta wave requires antegrade pathway conduction. Retrograde conduction can close an orthodromic reentry circuit even when antegrade conduction and resting ventricular activation are normal.

The pathway can provide the antegrade limb of antidromic AVRT: The demonstrated pathway has no antegrade conduction. It can return activation to the atrium but cannot itself provide the antegrade pre-excited limb required for antidromic AVRT.

options: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade accessory-pathway conduction

questions.explanation:
Recognition of Pre-Excited Atrial Fibrillation

Correct answer: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade accessory-pathway conduction

Pre-Excited AF

**Very rapid irregular rhythm with changing QRS width/morphology** suggests AF conducted through an accessory pathway.

Variable fusion of AV nodal and accessory conduction explains beat-to-beat changes.

Avoid AV Nodal Blockade

**AV nodal blockers can accelerate pathway-mediated ventricular activation and trigger VF.**

Avoid adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin and IV amiodarone in this setting.

**Unstable patients require electrical cardioversion.**

Stable cases may receive specialist-guided IV procainamide or ibutilide; consider definitive pathway ablation after stabilization.

Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Antidromic AVRT produces pre-excited wide complexes, but its reentrant cycle is ordinarily regular. The very irregular intervals and changing degrees of pre-excitation favor AF conducting through both available routes.

AF with fixed bundle-branch aberrancy: AF with bundle-branch disease can be irregular and wide, but fixed aberrancy generally preserves a more consistent conduction pattern. Known manifest pre-excitation and extreme variable ventricular activation raise concern for accessory conduction.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia: Polymorphic VT is an important dangerous wide-complex alternative. Here the prior delta wave and irregularly variable pre-excited pattern specifically support AF with accessory conduction, although diagnostic uncertainty must still be managed safely.

questions.question: During EPS for manifest pre-excitation, induced AF has a shortest pre-excited R–R interval of 220 ms. Which interpretation best matches ESC 2019 risk stratification?
options: The measurement primarily establishes slow retrograde pathway conduction
The measurement is reassuring because the average ventricular rate is lower
Risk cannot be assessed until a spontaneous clinical AF episode is recorded
The pathway has a high-risk antegrade conduction property supporting ablation discussion
questions.explanation:
High-Risk Accessory-Pathway Conduction

Correct answer: The pathway has a high-risk antegrade conduction property supporting ablation discussion

Accessory-Pathway Risk

**SPERRI ≤250 ms during AF is high risk under ESC 2019.**

SPERRI 220 ms demonstrates rapid antegrade pathway conduction; it is not an AV nodal refractory-period measurement.

Broader EPS Assessment

**Short pathway antegrade refractory period, multiple pathways and inducible AVRT** contribute to risk assessment.

**Catecholamines can expose faster conduction.**

Intermittent loss of pre-excitation can suggest lower risk but is not an absolute guarantee.

**Discuss ablation according to risk, occupation and patient preferences**, balancing pathway location and procedural hazards.

EPS finding | ESC 2019 high-risk feature

Shortest pre-excited RR during AF | ≤250 ms

Antegrade accessory-pathway ERP | ≤250 ms

Pathway number | Multiple accessory pathways

Inducibility | Accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia at baseline or catecholamine challenge

The measurement primarily establishes slow retrograde pathway conduction: The pre-excited R–R interval during AF reflects antegrade delivery to the ventricle. Slowly conducting retrograde pathways are relevant to PJRT but do not explain this rapid antegrade property.

The measurement is reassuring because the average ventricular rate is lower: SPERRI measures the fastest demonstrated pre-excited ventricular conduction rather than the average rate. Longer intervening intervals do not neutralize a documented very short pre-excited interval.

Risk cannot be assessed until a spontaneous clinical AF episode is recorded: Induced AF during a properly conducted EPS can assess pathway conduction. A spontaneous dangerous episode is not required before acting on a qualifying high-risk electrophysiological finding.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: Months after left atrial AF ablation, a patient develops sustained organized atrial tachycardia. The surface waves differ from classic inferior saw-tooth flutter. Prior CTI block remains intact. Which approach best defines the substrate before repeat ablation?
options: Create a mitral isthmus line solely from the history of left atrial ablation
Repeat the CTI line solely because the rhythm is called flutter
Select a focal ablation target solely because an isoelectric interval is visible
Activation and entrainment assessment to identify the actual atrial circuit and critical conduction channel
questions.explanation:
Atypical Scar-Related Atrial Flutter

Correct answer: Activation and entrainment assessment to identify the actual atrial circuit and critical conduction channel

Postablation Macroreentry

**Scar and lesion gaps can support non-CTI-dependent atrial reentry.**

Perimitral and roof-dependent circuits are examples; surface flutter morphology is unreliable after prior ablation.

Map Before Ablating

**Activation mapping plus appropriate entrainment identifies circuit participation and a critical isthmus.**

Account for the whole cycle and distinguish active circuit from passive activation.

**Intact CTI block does not exclude left atrial flutter.**

Empirical repetition of CTI ablation is poorly targeted when the clinical circuit lies elsewhere; assess lesion gaps and procedural risks.

Create a mitral isthmus line solely from the history of left atrial ablation: Perimitral reentry is plausible, but roof-dependent or other scar-related circuits can also occur. An empirical line without circuit definition may fail to address the rhythm and add further proarrhythmic gaps.

Repeat the CTI line solely because the rhythm is called flutter: A CTI line treats a demonstrated isthmus-dependent circuit. Intact block and a post-left-atrial-ablation substrate raise other possibilities; the generic flutter label does not establish a CTI gap.

Select a focal ablation target solely because an isoelectric interval is visible: A discrete-looking surface pattern can occur with scar-related macroreentry. An isoelectric interval does not prove focal origin when atrial activation is altered by prior lesions.

questions.question: A smartwatch using photoplethysmography repeatedly reports an irregular pulse in an asymptomatic adult. No ECG tracing has been recorded. Which next step is most appropriate before establishing a clinical AF diagnosis?
options: Use the absence of palpitations to dismiss the alerts
Diagnose AF from repeated optical alerts because repetition removes false positives
Obtain an interpretable ECG recording and have the rhythm reviewed by a qualified clinician
Use left atrial enlargement on echocardiography as confirmation
questions.explanation:
ECG Confirmation of Suspected Atrial Fibrillation

Correct answer: Obtain an interpretable ECG recording and have the rhythm reviewed by a qualified clinician

Confirm an Optical Alert

**Photoplethysmography detects pulse irregularity, not diagnostic atrial electrical activity.**

Obtain an interpretable ECG and clinician review before establishing clinical AF.

Recording Standards

**ESC 2024 accepts conventional 12-lead or interpretable single-/multilead ECG documentation.**

A usual ten-second 12-lead recording need not be extended to thirty seconds to count as that conventional recording.

**Longer ambulatory episodes require contextual interpretation.**

Duration, signal quality and clinical consequences guide further monitoring; an optical alert alone is not an anticoagulation mandate.

Use the absence of palpitations to dismiss the alerts: AF can be asymptomatic, so symptom absence cannot exclude it. The appropriate response is proportionate confirmatory recording rather than either immediate labelling or dismissal.

Diagnose AF from repeated optical alerts because repetition removes false positives: Repeated alerts increase the reason to investigate but do not convert pulse sensing into atrial electrical documentation. Ectopy and artefact can generate recurrent optical irregularity.

Use left atrial enlargement on echocardiography as confirmation: Atrial enlargement can identify substrate and influence management, but it is not rhythm documentation. Echo cannot establish that an optical alert represented AF rather than another irregular rhythm.

ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline, 2023 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

questions.question: During a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 165/min, atrial deflections continue independently at 78/min. An occasional narrow complex matching the baseline sinus QRS appears within the tachycardia. Which mechanism is most strongly supported?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia conducted with fixed bundle-branch block
Orthodromic AVRT with bundle-branch aberrancy
Ventricular tachycardia with intermittent sinus capture
Antidromic AVRT with variable pre-excitation
questions.explanation:
AV Dissociation and Capture During Wide-Complex Tachycardia

Correct answer: Ventricular tachycardia with intermittent sinus capture

VT-Supporting Signs

**AV dissociation plus a capture beat strongly supports VT.**

A sinus impulse occasionally reaches the ventricle when excitable, producing a near-normal narrow QRS within the wide tachycardia.

Capture, Fusion and Limits

**Fusion combines sinus and ventricular activation**, producing an intermediate QRS shape.

**Their absence does not exclude VT.**

P waves can be concealed, and VT may have 1:1 retrograde conduction.

**Treat uncertain regular wide tachycardia as VT**, especially with structural disease; instability requires immediate synchronized cardioversion when feasible.

Focal atrial tachycardia conducted with fixed bundle-branch block: An atrial driver would need to account for the faster ventricular activation. The observed atrial rate is slower and independent, while a sinus impulse occasionally captures the ventricle.

Orthodromic AVRT with bundle-branch aberrancy: AVRT requires coordinated atrial and ventricular participation in its reentrant loop. Independent slower atrial activity and an intervening sinus-capture complex oppose that ordinary circuit.

Antidromic AVRT with variable pre-excitation: Antidromic AVRT produces wide ventricular activation through an accessory pathway, but ordinary AVRT requires atrial participation. Slower dissociated atrial activity and sinus capture instead support an independent ventricular rhythm.

questions.question: A patient with previous MI has regular wide-complex tachycardia. No RS complex is present in any precordial lead. Atrial activity cannot be confidently identified. Which interpretation is best?
options: The tracing favors SVT because an RS-interval measurement is unavailable
The tracing favors SVT because atrial dissociation has not been demonstrated
The morphology supports VT; lack of visible AV dissociation does not negate that evidence
The absence of RS complexes establishes antidromic AVRT through an accessory pathway
questions.explanation:
Morphological Criteria in Regular Wide-Complex Tachycardia

Correct answer: The morphology supports VT; lack of visible AV dissociation does not negate that evidence

Wide-Complex Morphology

**No RS complex in any precordial lead is a Brugada-algorithm VT criterion.**

If RS exists, a longest RS interval >100 ms also supports VT; other steps assess AV dissociation and morphology.

Clinical Interpretation

**Prior MI markedly increases the likelihood of scar VT.**

Algorithms are probabilistic and have limitations with drugs, pre-excitation, metabolic disease and unusual substrates.

**Do not use a negative morphological rule to declare SVT certain.**

Compare baseline ECG, assess stability and avoid hazardous empirical AV nodal treatment in undifferentiated wide tachycardia.

The tracing favors SVT because an RS-interval measurement is unavailable: In the Brugada sequence, absence of RS complexes in all precordial leads itself supports VT. Measuring an RS interval is the next step when an RS complex exists, not a prerequisite for using the first criterion.

The tracing favors SVT because atrial dissociation has not been demonstrated: Visible dissociation strongly supports VT, but many VTs have concealed atrial activity or retrograde conduction. Its absence is not a positive criterion establishing supraventricular origin.

The absence of RS complexes establishes antidromic AVRT through an accessory pathway: Pre-excited tachycardia can mimic ventricular-origin morphology, so this remains a differential. Absence of precordial RS complexes does not establish accessory-pathway participation, particularly in a patient with an infarct substrate.

questions.question: Two monitored patients develop polymorphic VT. Between episodes, patient X has QTc 560 ms after a QT-prolonging drug and a pause preceding onset; patient Y has QTc 420 ms with acute ischemic chest pain. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Both most likely have CPVT because each has a polymorphic rhythm
Both have torsades because beat-to-beat QRS morphology varies
X most likely has ischemic polymorphic VT, while Y has drug-induced torsades
X has a torsades phenotype; Y requires assessment for ischemia-associated polymorphic VT rather than automatic torsades labelling
questions.explanation:
Torsades Versus Polymorphic VT With a Normal QT

Correct answer: X has a torsades phenotype; Y requires assessment for ischemia-associated polymorphic VT rather than automatic torsades labelling

Two Polymorphic Mechanisms

**Torsades is polymorphic VT with prolonged QT in the intervening rhythm.**

Pause-dependent onset after a QT-prolonging drug supports acquired torsades; normal-QT polymorphic VT during chest pain raises ischemic concern.

Mechanism-Specific Treatment

**Sustained polymorphic VT needs an unsynchronized shock**, because reliable synchronization is difficult.

**For acquired torsades:** stop culprit drugs, correct electrolytes and give IV magnesium; recurrent pause-dependent episodes may need rate acceleration.

**For normal-QT ischemic polymorphic VT:** urgently treat ischemia.

A twisting appearance alone does not justify diagnosing long-QT torsades.

Both most likely have CPVT because each has a polymorphic rhythm: CPVT is considered with adrenergically provoked bidirectional or polymorphic VT, typically with a normal resting ECG and no explanatory structural disease. Neither polymorphism alone nor these two supplied triggers establishes that inherited syndrome.

Both have torsades because beat-to-beat QRS morphology varies: Polymorphic morphology describes ventricular activation, but torsades specifically occurs in the setting of prolonged repolarization. Normal-QT polymorphic VT has a different etiological and treatment assessment.

X most likely has ischemic polymorphic VT, while Y has drug-induced torsades: The supplied interepisode QT and pause-dependent onset support acquired long-QT torsades in X. Acute ischemic symptoms with a normal QT support a different mechanism in Y rather than the reversed assignment.

questions.question: An older patient taking digoxin develops vomiting, new renal impairment and ventricular tachycardia with alternating frontal QRS axis on successive beats. The resting QT before the episode was not prolonged. Which cause is most likely?
options: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Digoxin toxicity
Acquired long-QT torsades de pointes
Scar-related monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Bidirectional Ventricular Tachycardia in Clinical Context

Correct answer: Digoxin toxicity

Bidirectional VT

**Alternating frontal QRS axis on successive beats** defines the pattern.

Digoxin toxicity, CPVT and Andersen–Tawil syndrome are important associations; the pattern is not synonymous with torsades.

Use the Clinical Context

**Digoxin exposure, vomiting and new renal dysfunction favor toxicity here.**

CPVT typically appears with adrenergic stress in a younger structurally normal heart.

**Stop digoxin and assess perfusion, renal function and electrolytes urgently.**

Life-threatening digoxin-related ventricular arrhythmia warrants digoxin immune Fab and specialist support; do not rely on an isolated level to delay treatment.

Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia: CPVT can produce bidirectional VT, usually during adrenergic stress in a patient without explanatory structural disease. New renal impairment, digoxin exposure and gastrointestinal symptoms make an acquired toxic mechanism more likely here.

Acquired long-QT torsades de pointes: Drug-induced torsades is associated with prolonged repolarization and commonly pause-dependent polymorphic VT. Alternation between two ventricular axes with a previously normal QT and this exposure history favors digoxin toxicity.

Scar-related monomorphic ventricular tachycardia: Scar reentry is important in structural heart disease and generally produces a stable monomorphic pattern during a given episode. Beat-to-beat axis alternation and systemic digoxin-toxicity clues require a different explanation.

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

Digoxin prescribing information, 2025 — https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/009330s040lbl.pdf

questions.question: Years after MI, a patient has recurrent sustained monomorphic VT. Induced clinical VT causes hypotension too rapidly for prolonged activation mapping. Which approach best explains a useful ablation strategy?
options: Target the earliest isolated PVC as the presumed source of the sustained scar VT
Restrict mapping to prolonged activation and entrainment during the hypotensive clinical VT
Map abnormal scar channels and electrograms during a tolerated rhythm to target the reentry substrate
Use a single pace-map match as proof of the entire critical reentry isthmus
questions.explanation:
Scar Reentry and Substrate Mapping

Correct answer: Map abnormal scar channels and electrograms during a tolerated rhythm to target the reentry substrate

Scar-Reentry Substrate

**Surviving myocardial channels within/along scar permit slow conduction and reentry.**

Postinfarction monomorphic VT is not simply electrical activity arising from uniformly dead tissue.

Mapping When VT Is Intolerable

**Substrate mapping in sinus or paced rhythm identifies abnormal potentials and conduction channels.**

Activation/entrainment mapping is useful when VT is tolerated; prolonged induced hypotension is not required to locate a target.

**Ablation strategy remains individualized.**

Integrate imaging, electrograms and induced rhythm information, with hemodynamic support and recurrence prevention when appropriate.

Target the earliest isolated PVC as the presumed source of the sustained scar VT: Activation mapping of a trigger PVC is valuable for selected focal arrhythmias or PVC-triggered VF. In established scar reentry, an incidental PVC need not identify the critical sustaining channel and cannot substitute for circuit or substrate assessment.

Restrict mapping to prolonged activation and entrainment during the hypotensive clinical VT: Activation and entrainment are useful when VT can be sustained safely. Repeated prolonged induction in this poorly tolerated rhythm can worsen perfusion; substrate mapping provides information during a more tolerable rhythm.

Use a single pace-map match as proof of the entire critical reentry isthmus: Pace mapping can identify an exit region or support localization. A matching surface QRS does not by itself prove participation of that site in the essential channel or define the full circuit.

questions.question: A young adult has catecholamine-associated monomorphic VT with an LBBB-like pattern and inferior axis. Baseline ECG, echo and directed structural evaluation are reassuring. Adenosine terminates a monitored episode. Which interpretation is most likely?
options: Scar-mediated macroreentrant VT established by the broad QRS
Typical slow–fast AVNRT established by adenosine termination
Left posterior fascicular reentrant VT
Idiopathic outflow-tract VT, commonly related to cAMP-mediated triggered activity
questions.explanation:
Outflow-Tract Ventricular Tachycardia

Correct answer: Idiopathic outflow-tract VT, commonly related to cAMP-mediated triggered activity

Idiopathic RVOT VT

**LBBB-like morphology with inferior axis** commonly reflects activation from a superior right-ventricular source.

Many cases involve cAMP-dependent calcium loading and delayed-afterdepolarization triggered activity.

Interpret Adenosine Response

**Adenosine can terminate selected outflow VTs.**

Response does not prove that a tachycardia is supraventricular; rate and drug response are not sufficient classifiers.

**Exclude structural/inherited disease before calling it idiopathic.**

ARVC and other RV substrates can mimic the surface pattern; assess ECG, imaging, family history and symptoms. Recurrent symptomatic disease may benefit from ablation.

Scar-mediated macroreentrant VT established by the broad QRS: Scar reentry is important when structural disease is present. QRS width alone does not establish scar, and this selected reassuring evaluation and adenosine-sensitive outflow phenotype favor triggered idiopathic VT.

Typical slow–fast AVNRT established by adenosine termination: AVNRT often terminates with adenosine, but some ventricular tachycardias do as well. The demonstrated ventricular phenotype and outflow-type morphology require interpretation rather than assigning a nodal mechanism from the drug response alone.

Left posterior fascicular reentrant VT: The common posterior fascicular phenotype has an RBBB-like pattern and superior or leftward axis and is typically verapamil sensitive. The supplied LBBB-like inferior-axis pattern and adrenergic association favor an outflow source.

ESC ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

HRS/EHRA/APHRS/LAHRS ventricular arrhythmia ablation consensus, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1002/joa3.12185

questions.question: A young adult has recurrent tolerated VT with an RBBB-like QRS and superior axis. Structural evaluation is reassuring, and a previous EPS established posterior fascicular reentry. Which acute drug can specifically terminate this mechanism when pressure and conduction permit?
options: IV amiodarone
IV adenosine
IV diltiazem
IV verapamil under continuous monitoring
questions.explanation:
Verapamil-Sensitive Fascicular Ventricular Tachycardia

Correct answer: IV verapamil under continuous monitoring

Posterior Fascicular VT

**RBBB-like QRS with superior axis** is typical of posterior fascicular reentry.

Specialized Purkinje tissue participates, so QRS may be relatively narrow for VT.

Verapamil Requires a Known Mechanism

**IV verapamil can terminate established, tolerated verapamil-sensitive fascicular VT.**

Monitor pressure and conduction; this is not an empirical diagnostic trial for an uncertain wide rhythm.

**Unstable tachycardia needs electrical treatment.**

Recurrent fascicular VT can be treated by catheter ablation; reconsider structural disease if the phenotype or imaging is atypical.

IV amiodarone: Amiodarone is a general option for selected tolerated ventricular tachycardias and may have antiarrhythmic effects here. The question asks for the specific established sensitivity of this confirmed fascicular circuit, for which verapamil is preferred.

IV adenosine: Adenosine treats AV-node-dependent SVT and can terminate selected triggered outflow VT. Reentrant posterior fascicular VT is characteristically verapamil sensitive rather than defined by adenosine sensitivity.

IV diltiazem: Diltiazem is useful for selected supraventricular rate-control problems, but membership in the nondihydropyridine calcium-channel-blocker group does not establish equivalent efficacy for fascicular reentry. Verapamil is the established mechanism-directed agent here.

questions.question: An asymptomatic adult has stable terminal QRS notching with 1.5-mm J-point elevation in two contiguous inferior leads. There is no syncope, premature familial sudden death or documented ventricular arrhythmia, and directed assessment is reassuring. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Short-QT syndrome is established by terminal QRS notching
Early-repolarization syndrome is established by the inferior-lead distribution alone
A type 1 Brugada pattern is established because J-point elevation exceeds one millimeter
An early-repolarization ECG pattern is present; the tracing alone does not establish early-repolarization syndrome or an ICD indication
questions.explanation:
Early Repolarization Pattern Versus Arrhythmic Syndrome

Correct answer: An early-repolarization ECG pattern is present; the tracing alone does not establish early-repolarization syndrome or an ICD indication

Early Repolarization Pattern

**Terminal QRS notching/slurring with J elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 adjacent inferior/lateral leads** describes the pattern.

It is common in healthy people; inferior high-amplitude/horizontal-ST phenotypes may carry greater population risk.

Pattern Is Not Syndrome

**Early-repolarization syndrome concerns otherwise unexplained polymorphic VT/VF in a patient with the pattern.**

The supplied asymptomatic adult has no such event, so the ECG alone does not establish that syndrome.

**Use symptoms and family history to guide assessment.**

Do not label new ischemic chest pain benign merely because an earlier tracing had early repolarization.

Finding | What is needed for interpretation

Inferolateral J-point notch/slur | Pattern assessment plus symptoms and family history

Type 1 Brugada | Coved right-precordial morphology and clinical context

Short QT | Reliable QT measurement, secondary-cause exclusion and phenotype assessment

Short-QT syndrome is established by terminal QRS notching: Short-QT syndrome concerns abbreviated repolarization assessed through QT and clinical context. Terminal QRS notching does not establish a short QT or its associated syndrome.

Early-repolarization syndrome is established by the inferior-lead distribution alone: Inferior distribution can contribute to risk assessment, but a pattern is not the same as a clinical arrhythmic syndrome. The ECG finding alone does not supply the missing ventricular event.

A type 1 Brugada pattern is established because J-point elevation exceeds one millimeter: Brugada type 1 requires a specific coved right-precordial morphology, not generic inferior J-point elevation. Lead location and morphology distinguish the patterns.

questions.question: A young person has exertional syncope, a normal resting QTc and normal cardiac imaging. Monitored exercise produces increasing ventricular ectopy followed by bidirectional and polymorphic VT. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Congenital long QT syndrome as the best fit
Idiopathic RV outflow tract VT
Brugada syndrome
questions.explanation:
Exercise-Provoked Polymorphic Arrhythmia With Normal Resting ECG

Correct answer: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia

Electrical Phenotype

**Resting ECG may be normal.**

Adrenergic stress reveals abnormal intracellular calcium handling; RYR2 is a common genetic cause, with other genes including CASQ2.

Management

**Specialist inherited-arrhythmia care**, exercise/trigger counseling and nonselective beta-blockade, often nadolol.

**Add flecainide for persistent arrhythmias** despite appropriate beta-blockade; assess left cardiac sympathetic denervation in refractory cases.

**ICD decisions are individualized**, especially after arrest or refractory events.

Shocks can provoke adrenergic escalation; an ICD does not replace medication or specialist follow-up.

Congenital long QT syndrome as the best fit: LQTS can cause exertional events and occasionally a normal resting QT, but progressive adrenergic bidirectional/polymorphic ectopy with normal structure is especially characteristic of CPVT.

Idiopathic RV outflow tract VT: RVOT VT is usually monomorphic with a consistent LBBB/inferior-axis morphology, unlike the escalating bidirectional/polymorphic pattern.

Brugada syndrome: Brugada events more often occur at rest/fever with a diagnostic right-precordial pattern; this exercise-dependent calcium-handling phenotype fits CPVT better.

ESC Ventricular Arrhythmia/Sudden Death Guideline, 2022 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehac262

questions.question: During an ARVC evaluation, a 24-year-old has T-wave inversion in V1–V3 and no complete RBBB. Under the revised 2010 Task Force framework, which interpretation is appropriate?
options: One major depolarization criterion
One minor repolarization criterion
One major repolarization criterion
One minor depolarization criterion
questions.explanation:
ARVC ECG Criteria and Conduction Exclusions

Correct answer: One major repolarization criterion

Named 2010 Repolarization Criterion

**T inversion in V1–V3 or beyond in age >14 without complete RBBB is a major 2010 ARVC criterion.**

The stem explicitly uses that framework; T inversion is a repolarization finding, not an epsilon wave.

Avoid Single-Sign Diagnosis

**ARVC diagnosis combines structural, tissue, rhythm, ECG and familial/genetic evidence.**

Other diseases, athlete patterns and technical errors must be considered.

**Complete RBBB changes criterion interpretation.**

Confirm lead placement and reproducibility; an isolated major ECG criterion does not alone establish definite ARVC or an ICD indication.

One major depolarization criterion: T-wave inversion concerns repolarization. A reproducible epsilon wave was a major delayed-activation finding in the 2010 framework, but no such post-QRS signal is supplied here.

One minor repolarization criterion: Adult V1–V2 inversion without complete RBBB can be a minor finding, while the supplied extension through V3 meets the major rule. The separate complete-RBBB context uses different lead requirements.

One minor depolarization criterion: Terminal activation delay and selected signal-averaged ECG abnormalities are minor delayed-activation findings. They require their own measurements and cannot be inferred from the supplied T-wave inversion.

Revised ARVC Task Force diagnostic criteria, 2010 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehq025

questions.question: A patient with advanced CKD has confirmed nonhemolyzed potassium 7.0 mmol/L, but QRS duration and T waves are not strikingly abnormal. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A normal-looking ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalemia or remove the need for urgent treatment
The potassium result must be artifactual because ECG changes are absent
Treatment can wait until QRS widening appears
Only calcium is needed because it removes potassium rapidly
questions.explanation:
Hyperkalemia With a Reassuring ECG

Correct answer: A normal-looking ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalemia or remove the need for urgent treatment

ECG Limitations

**ECG sensitivity is limited**, and severity depends on rate of rise, acid–base state and underlying disease.

Peaked T waves, loss of P waves and QRS widening are important when present but may not progress sequentially.

Urgent Management

**Monitor, confirm the context and treat the severe biochemical abnormality.**

Use appropriate intracellular-shift measures and potassium removal, including dialysis when indicated; monitor glucose with insulin therapy.

**Calcium is membrane stabilization**, especially with toxic ECG changes or instability, rather than potassium removal.

**Recheck potassium and watch rebound** after temporary shifting treatments.

The potassium result must be artifactual because ECG changes are absent: Pseudohyperkalemia requires sampling/clinical assessment; a confirmed result cannot be dismissed solely because the ECG lacks classic changes.

Treatment can wait until QRS widening appears: ECG changes do not follow a reliable obligatory sequence; waiting for conduction failure risks sudden deterioration.

Only calcium is needed because it removes potassium rapidly: IV calcium stabilizes the myocardium when indicated but does not lower total body potassium; shifting and elimination strategies address the potassium burden.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/

questions.question: After prolonged vomiting, a patient has flat T waves, ST depression and large U waves in V2–V4. The machine reports QTc 610 ms, but T and U are partly fused. What is the best interpretation?
options: Hypokalemic repolarization abnormality with possible QU mismeasurement
Definite congenital long QT syndrome based on the machine value
Hypercalcemia shortening the ST segment
Therapeutic digoxin effect as the complete explanation
questions.explanation:
Hypokalemia and Apparent QT Prolongation

Correct answer: Hypokalemic repolarization abnormality with possible QU mismeasurement

Measurement

**Exclude a separate U wave from QT.**

When T–U fusion obscures the endpoint, use a clearer lead and manual assessment; the machine may have measured QU.

Clinical Response

**Check potassium, magnesium and renal function**, replace deficits and review QT-prolonging drugs.

Hypomagnesemia can cause refractory potassium depletion and increase ventricular arrhythmia risk.

**Do not dismiss the tracing as merely a measurement error.**

Hypokalemia itself promotes ectopy and torsades; monitor severe abnormalities and reassess the ECG after correction.

Definite congenital long QT syndrome based on the machine value: Acquired electrolyte depletion and unclear T-wave end must be addressed before diagnosing an inherited syndrome from an automated number.

Hypercalcemia shortening the ST segment: Hypercalcemia generally shortens QT through ST shortening; flat T waves and prominent U waves after vomiting favor potassium depletion.

Therapeutic digoxin effect as the complete explanation: Digoxin may cause scooped ST depression and shorter QT, but the supplied GI-loss context and prominent U waves require electrolyte assessment.

AHA ECG Monitoring Practice Standards, 2017 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000527

questions.question: A patient has a markedly abbreviated ST segment and short QT, with otherwise relatively preserved T-wave morphology. Which biochemical abnormality most directly explains this pattern?
options: Hypocalcemia
Hypercalcemia
Hypokalemia
Hypomagnesemia
questions.explanation:
Calcium and the ST Segment

Correct answer: Hypercalcemia

Repolarization Mechanism

**High calcium shortens the ventricular plateau**, abbreviating ST and QT.

Low calcium prolongs ST; the effect need not require a major change in T-wave duration.

Confirm and Distinguish

**Measure calcium and assess the clinical cause.**

Albumin and ionized calcium may matter; ECG cannot quantify the biochemical level.

**Short QT also occurs with digoxin or rare inherited disease.**

Exclude acquired causes before diagnosing short QT syndrome; severe hypercalcemia can also cause PR/QRS changes or bradyarrhythmia.

Hypocalcemia: Low calcium prolongs the plateau/ST segment and QT, producing the opposite direction of change.

Hypokalemia: Potassium depletion typically produces flat T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves rather than isolated ST shortening.

Hypomagnesemia: Magnesium depletion promotes arrhythmias and often accompanies QT-related risk; a very short ST segment points more directly to increased calcium.

AHA/ACCF/HRS ECG Standardization, Part I — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2007.01.024

questions.question: After amitriptyline ingestion, a patient develops hypotension, QRS 148 ms and a prominent terminal R wave in aVR. Which treatment most directly targets the conduction toxicity?
options: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Intravenous magnesium as the sole targeted therapy
Intravenous amiodarone as the initial targeted treatment
Intravenous calcium gluconate as the principal antidote
questions.explanation:
Sodium-Channel Blocker Cardiotoxicity

Correct answer: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate

Toxic ECG Pattern

**Fast sodium-channel blockade slows phase-0 conduction**, widening QRS and shifting terminal forces toward aVR.

Seizures, acidosis and shock can worsen toxicity; do not wait for a drug level.

Resuscitation

**IV sodium bicarbonate boluses are titrated to improved QRS width and perfusion.**

Common initial dosing is 1–2 mEq/kg; monitor sodium, potassium and blood gas to avoid excessive alkalemia/hypernatremia.

**Support ventilation and circulation and treat seizures**, with poison-center/critical-care involvement.

**Continuous ECG reassessment is essential.**

A transient response does not establish toxin clearance; ongoing therapy depends on recurrent conduction toxicity and hemodynamics.

Intravenous magnesium as the sole targeted therapy: Magnesium is central in torsades with delayed repolarization; this pattern instead identifies sodium-channel conduction blockade requiring sodium/alkalinization therapy.

Intravenous amiodarone as the initial targeted treatment: Amiodarone is used for selected arrhythmias, but it does not reverse the toxic sodium-channel mechanism and can add hypotension or electrophysiological effects.

Intravenous calcium gluconate as the principal antidote: Calcium is used for hyperkalemic membrane stabilization or selected calcium-channel blocker poisoning; it is not the principal treatment for TCA conduction toxicity.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation: Poisoning — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/
questions.explanationHtml:
Sodium-Channel Blocker Cardiotoxicity

Correct answer: A — Intravenous sodium bicarbonate

Toxic ECG Pattern

  • Fast sodium-channel blockade slows phase-0 conduction, widening QRS and shifting terminal forces toward aVR.
    • Seizures, acidosis and shock can worsen toxicity; do not wait for a drug level.

Resuscitation

  • IV sodium bicarbonate boluses are titrated to improved QRS width and perfusion.
    • Common initial dosing is 1–2 mEq/kg; monitor sodium, potassium and blood gas to avoid excessive alkalemia/hypernatremia.
  • Support ventilation and circulation and treat seizures, with poison-center/critical-care involvement.
  • Continuous ECG reassessment is essential.
    • A transient response does not establish toxin clearance; ongoing therapy depends on recurrent conduction toxicity and hemodynamics.

Other Options

  • B — Intravenous magnesium as the sole targeted therapy: Magnesium is central in torsades with delayed repolarization; this pattern instead identifies sodium-channel conduction blockade requiring sodium/alkalinization therapy.
  • C — Intravenous amiodarone as the initial targeted treatment: Amiodarone is used for selected arrhythmias, but it does not reverse the toxic sodium-channel mechanism and can add hypotension or electrophysiological effects.
  • D — Intravenous calcium gluconate as the principal antidote: Calcium is used for hyperkalemic membrane stabilization or selected calcium-channel blocker poisoning; it is not the principal treatment for TCA conduction toxicity.

References

  • AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation: Poisoning

questions.question: A stable patient taking digoxin has unchanged scooped lateral ST depression, mildly prolonged PR and a shortened QT. There are no new symptoms, ectopy or conduction block. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Therapeutic digoxin-related repolarization and AV nodal effects
Definite digoxin toxicity requiring antibody fragments
Acute subendocardial ischemia established by ST shape alone
Hypokalemia as the necessary explanation
questions.explanation:
Therapeutic Digoxin Effect

Correct answer: Therapeutic digoxin-related repolarization and AV nodal effects

Drug Effect Versus Toxicity

**Digoxin effect:** scooped ST depression, QT shortening and vagally mediated PR prolongation.

This pattern can occur at therapeutic exposure and is not a serum-level assay.

When to Suspect Toxicity

**New GI/neurological symptoms, ectopy or AV block** require reassessment.

Atrial tachycardia with block and bidirectional VT are important toxic patterns.

**Check renal function, potassium, magnesium and interacting drugs.**

Interpret a serum level with sampling time and clinical context; treat life-threatening toxicity rather than the ST shape alone.

Definite digoxin toxicity requiring antibody fragments: Toxicity requires integrated clinical/rhythm evidence; the stable characteristic repolarization effect alone does not establish life-threatening poisoning.

Acute subendocardial ischemia established by ST shape alone: Ischemia can coexist, but an unchanged characteristic drug pattern without ischemic symptoms does not establish acute coronary disease.

Hypokalemia as the necessary explanation: Hypokalemia can increase digoxin toxicity and produces U waves/flat T waves; it is not required to explain this stable therapeutic drug pattern.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/

questions.question: A patient rescued after prolonged cold exposure has a core temperature of 29°C, sinus bradycardia and a prominent positive deflection at the QRS–ST junction in several leads. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Acute territorial ST-elevation infarction
Hypothermia-associated Osborn waves
Brugada type 1 pattern
Hyperkalemia as the sole mechanism
questions.explanation:
Hypothermic J Waves

Correct answer: Hypothermia-associated Osborn waves

ECG Effects

**Hypothermia can produce J waves, bradycardia and prolonged intervals.**

J-wave size often increases as temperature falls; shivering artifact may obscure the tracing.

Clinical Care

**Use controlled rewarming and continuous monitoring**, with gentle handling and correction of associated metabolic abnormalities.

**J waves are not absolutely specific to hypothermia.**

Interpret temperature, lead distribution and symptoms; reassess persistent abnormalities after rewarming.

**Severe hypothermia increases ventricular arrhythmia risk**, so the tracing should trigger appropriate resuscitation planning rather than isolated ECG labeling.

Acute territorial ST-elevation infarction: Acute occlusion remains a clinical differential, but diffuse J-point deflections with severe hypothermia and bradycardia fit temperature-related changes better than a single coronary territory.

Brugada type 1 pattern: Brugada requires characteristic coved right-precordial ST elevation with T inversion in the relevant context; generalized hypothermic J waves are not equivalent.

Hyperkalemia as the sole mechanism: Hyperkalemia commonly alters T waves, P waves and QRS conduction; the temperature-dependent QRS–ST notch is a characteristic hypothermic clue.

AHA Special Circumstances of Resuscitation — https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-and-pediatric-special-circumstances-of-resuscitation/

questions.question: A pacemaker-dependent patient becomes presyncopal. Ventricular pacing spikes occur regularly, but several are not followed by QRS complexes. What is the immediate device abnormality?
options: Ventricular oversensing
Failure of ventricular capture
Ventricular undersensing
Normal fusion beats
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker Failure to Capture

Correct answer: Failure of ventricular capture

Recognize Noncapture

**Output is present but myocardial activation is absent.**

Causes include lead displacement/failure, rising threshold, metabolic disturbance and inadequate programmed output.

Urgent Response

**Assess perfusion and provide backup pacing/resuscitation if unstable.**

A pacemaker-dependent patient can deteriorate rapidly; do not wait for routine clinic follow-up.

**Arrange urgent interrogation**, check leads and reversible causes such as hyperkalemia/acidosis.

Output adjustment may restore capture, but correcting lead or metabolic pathology is essential; verify mechanical as well as electrical response.

Ventricular oversensing: Oversensing generally inhibits expected output, causing absent spikes; here stimuli are visible but fail to depolarize the ventricle.

Ventricular undersensing: Undersensing causes inappropriate pacing despite intrinsic beats; it does not primarily describe a delivered stimulus lacking the expected QRS.

Normal fusion beats: Fusion combines intrinsic and paced activation into a QRS; a spike with no ventricular depolarization is not a fusion complex.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: A patient with a ventricular demand pacemaker develops pauses during arm movement. Interrogation shows rapid nonphysiological sensed signals and suppression of ventricular output during the pauses. What mechanism best fits?
options: Undersensing of intrinsic QRS complexes
Failure of myocardial capture
Oversensing of lead-related noise
Normal rate-responsive pacing
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker Oversensing

Correct answer: Oversensing of lead-related noise

Mechanism

**Inappropriate sensing resets/inhibits demand pacing.**

Lead fracture, insulation problems, myopotentials or electromagnetic interference can produce noise; movement association helps localize the cause.

Management

**Assess dependence and instability**, provide backup support and obtain urgent device interrogation.

**Review stored electrograms, impedance and lead integrity.**

Intermittent faults can escape a single normal measurement.

**Magnet responses differ by device and programming.**

Do not assume that a magnet universally creates safe asynchronous pacing, especially in ICDs; use a device-specific supervised plan.

Undersensing of intrinsic QRS complexes: Undersensing typically permits unnecessary pacing because intrinsic activity is missed; the device is instead detecting excessive inappropriate signals.

Failure of myocardial capture: Capture failure requires delivered pacing stimuli without depolarization; output is being inhibited before a stimulus is delivered here.

Normal rate-responsive pacing: Rate-response algorithms increase or adjust pacing with activity; they do not normally interpret lead noise as repeated intrinsic ventricular beats causing pauses.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: In a dual-chamber pacemaker, a ventricular premature beat is followed by retrograde atrial activation. Each subsequent atrial sensed event triggers ventricular pacing after the programmed AV delay, at the upper tracking rate. What mechanism best fits?
options: Sensor-driven rate-responsive tachycardia
Endless-loop pacemaker-mediated tachycardia
Atrial flutter tracking
Ventricular tachycardia with incidental pacemaker spikes
questions.explanation:
Pacemaker-Mediated Tachycardia

Correct answer: Endless-loop pacemaker-mediated tachycardia

Circuit

**Retrograde VA conduction + atrial sensing + ventricular tracking** completes the loop.

A PVC or loss of AV synchrony can initiate it; rate is often limited by the upper tracking setting.

Terminate and Prevent

**Device interrogation confirms the sequence.**

Programming a sufficiently long postventricular atrial refractory period prevents tracking of the retrograde P wave; PMT termination algorithms can help.

**Distinguish true atrial tachyarrhythmia and sensor-driven pacing** before reprogramming.

Review VA timing and preserve appropriate exercise tracking; do not treat every paced tachycardia as intrinsic VT.

Sensor-driven rate-responsive tachycardia: Sensor-driven acceleration follows the activity/physiological sensor rather than a stable retrograde atrial–ventricular tracking loop initiated by a PVC.

Atrial flutter tracking: Flutter tracking originates from an independent rapid atrial rhythm; here each atrial signal follows ventricular activation retrogradely.

Ventricular tachycardia with incidental pacemaker spikes: The device is triggering each ventricular event after sensed atrial activity, supporting a device-mediated loop rather than an independent ventricular focus.

ESC Cardiac Pacing and CRT Guideline, 2021 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

questions.question: During venepuncture, a patient becomes nauseated and pale, collapses, has several brief irregular jerks, and is oriented within seconds after being placed supine. Which interpretation is most likely?
options: Psychogenic pseudosyncope solely because venepuncture is a trigger
Generalized tonic-clonic seizure established by any jerking
Reflex syncope with hypoperfusion-related myoclonic movements
Cataplexy
questions.explanation:
Convulsive Syncope Versus Epileptic Seizure

Correct answer: Reflex syncope with hypoperfusion-related myoclonic movements

Discriminating History

**Trigger, autonomic prodrome and rapid reorientation** support reflex syncope.

Brief arrhythmic jerks and urinary incontinence can occur in either syncope or seizure.

Avoid a Duration Myth

**Generalized tonic-clonic seizures often last about 1–2 minutes**, followed by postictal impairment; they do not usually require >5 minutes to qualify.

Lateral tongue bite, stereotyped aura and prolonged confusion favor seizure, but no isolated sign replaces the full account.

**Obtain witness history, examination, orthostatic vitals and ECG.**

Target EEG or neurological investigations to a credible seizure suspicion rather than reflexively ordering them for all fainting.

Psychogenic pseudosyncope solely because venepuncture is a trigger: Emotional/procedural triggers can cause genuine reflex hypotension; a functional diagnosis needs positive features and appropriate physiological correlation.

Generalized tonic-clonic seizure established by any jerking: Brief myoclonus can occur during cerebral hypoperfusion; movements alone do not establish epilepsy when the trigger, pallor and rapid recovery favor syncope.

Cataplexy: Cataplexy causes emotion-triggered loss of tone with preserved awareness; this event includes true transient loss of consciousness and presyncopal autonomic symptoms.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

questions.question: After five minutes supine, BP is 142/82 mmHg. At one and three minutes of standing it is 116/72 and 114/70, with reproduced lightheadedness. Which diagnosis is supported?
options: Classical orthostatic hypotension
Initial orthostatic hypotension
Delayed orthostatic hypotension
POTS
questions.explanation:
Classical Orthostatic Hypotension

Correct answer: Classical orthostatic hypotension

Threshold and Timing

**Sustained SBP fall ≥20 or DBP fall ==≥10 mmHg== within 3 minutes** meets the classical threshold.

The wording is within three minutes, not only a measurement after three minutes; ESC also recognizes sustained SBP ==<90 mmHg==.

Determine the Cause

**Review volume, drugs and autonomic symptoms.**

Blunted HR compensation can suggest neurogenic disease, but beta-blockers, pacing and conduction disease confound it.

**Treat reversible contributors first**, then consider fluid/salt measures and compression when safe.

Supine hypertension, heart failure and renal disease limit indiscriminate volume expansion.

Initial orthostatic hypotension: Initial OH is a transient marked fall within roughly 15 seconds of standing; a sustained fall at one and three minutes fits classical OH.

Delayed orthostatic hypotension: Delayed OH begins beyond three minutes; the clinically significant fall is already present within the first minute.

POTS: POTS requires orthostatic tachycardia without a sustained OH-range pressure fall; this patient has a clear sustained hypotensive response.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071

questions.question: A 24-year-old has six months of upright palpitations and lightheadedness relieved by lying down. HR rises from 70 to 108/min on repeated standing measurements within ten minutes; BP remains stable. Anemia, dehydration, thyroid disease and medication effects are excluded. Which diagnosis best fits?
options: Classical orthostatic hypotension
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome
Inappropriate sinus tachycardia
Paroxysmal AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome

Correct answer: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

Required Features

**Sustained HR rise ≥30/min in adults** within ten minutes; ≥40/min for ages 12–19.

Require chronic orthostatic symptoms, generally ≥3 months, no sustained OH-range BP fall and no better explanation.

Assessment and Care

**Repeat standardized supine-to-standing HR/BP measurements.**

A single transient peak is insufficient; consider morning variability and confounders.

**Begin individualized fluid/salt, compression and graded exercise measures** when appropriate.

Medication selection depends on HR, pressure and symptoms; POTS is not diagnosed solely from a wearable pulse alert or from unexplained fatigue.

Classical orthostatic hypotension: Classical OH requires a sustained pressure fall; stable BP with a sustained symptomatic tachycardic response supports a different orthostatic syndrome.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia: IST more often includes excessive resting/average heart rate and symptoms beyond posture; a normal supine HR with a reproducible upright response favors POTS.

Paroxysmal AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT typically starts and stops abruptly as a reentrant rhythm; the sustained posture-linked sinus acceleration described here is not that pattern.

Canadian Cardiovascular Society Position Statement on POTS, 2020 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cjca.2019.12.024

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071

    • Require chronic orthostatic symptoms, generally ≥3 months, no sustained OH-range BP fall and no better explanation.

Assessment and Care

  • Repeat standardized supine-to-standing HR/BP measurements.
    • A single transient peak is insufficient; consider morning variability and confounders.
  • Begin individualized fluid/salt, compression and graded exercise measures when appropriate.
    • Medication selection depends on HR, pressure and symptoms; POTS is not diagnosed solely from a wearable pulse alert or from unexplained fatigue.

Other Options

  • A — Classical orthostatic hypotension: Classical OH requires a sustained pressure fall; stable BP with a sustained symptomatic tachycardic response supports a different orthostatic syndrome.
  • C — Inappropriate sinus tachycardia: IST more often includes excessive resting/average heart rate and symptoms beyond posture; a normal supine HR with a reproducible upright response favors POTS.
  • D — Paroxysmal AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT typically starts and stops abruptly as a reentrant rhythm; the sustained posture-linked sinus acceleration described here is not that pattern.

References

  • Canadian Cardiovascular Society Position Statement on POTS, 2020
  • ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018

questions.question: A patient has recurrent unexplained syncope every three to four months. Initial assessment and echo are unrevealing, and there is no indication for immediate ICD/pacing or inpatient high-risk treatment. Which strategy best seeks symptom–rhythm correlation?
options: A single 24-hour Holter recording
Implantable loop recorder
A 48-hour inpatient telemetry admission as the definitive long-term test
Routine invasive EPS in every such patient
questions.explanation:
Monitoring Infrequent Unexplained Syncope

Correct answer: Implantable loop recorder

Match Monitoring to Event Frequency

**Long-term recording increases the chance of capturing the spontaneous event.**

The objective is a rhythm correlated with symptoms, not merely incidental ectopy.

Selection and Interpretation

**ILR is appropriate in selected recurrent unexplained syncope** when recurrence is likely and immediate high-risk therapy is not required.

**A normal short monitor does not exclude arrhythmia.**

External monitoring suits sufficiently frequent episodes; high-risk findings require prompt evaluation rather than waiting months for an ILR event.

**Continue assessment for nonarrhythmic causes** even after implantation.

A single 24-hour Holter recording: Holter is useful when symptoms are frequent; a one-day window is unlikely to capture an event recurring every few months.

A 48-hour inpatient telemetry admission as the definitive long-term test: Telemetry is appropriate for immediate high-risk assessment but a brief admission has low yield for this infrequent stable recurrence pattern.

Routine invasive EPS in every such patient: EPS is useful in selected substrates or conduction disease; it is not the highest-yield universal test in a structurally reassuring, infrequent-event presentation.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

questions.question: A patient with an uncertain history has typical symptoms reproduced on tilt, preceded by progressive hypotension and then bradycardia. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The result demonstrates susceptibility to a reflex hypotensive response, interpreted with the spontaneous history
It excludes an arrhythmic cause for every previous event
It establishes a pacemaker indication from hypotension alone
It establishes epilepsy because consciousness was lost during testing
questions.explanation:
Interpreting a Positive Tilt Test

Correct answer: The result demonstrates susceptibility to a reflex hypotensive response, interpreted with the spontaneous history

Physiological Meaning

**Tilt reproduces symptoms with monitored HR and BP.**

The timing of hypotension versus bradycardia helps characterize vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory or mixed responses.

Limits

**A positive result is contextual evidence**, not a universal explanation of every attack.

A negative result does not exclude reflex syncope either.

**Tilt can also evaluate delayed OH or apparent functional events** using appropriate physiological recording.

**Use the spontaneous history and risk profile** to decide whether additional rhythm or structural assessment is still needed.

It excludes an arrhythmic cause for every previous event: Reflex susceptibility can coexist with cardiac disease; a positive tilt does not prove that all spontaneous episodes share the same mechanism.

It establishes a pacemaker indication from hypotension alone: Pacing targets selected cardioinhibitory mechanisms and cannot directly reverse vasodilation; tilt-induced hypotension alone is not sufficient.

It establishes epilepsy because consciousness was lost during testing: Loss of consciousness with documented hypotension/bradycardia supports hypoperfusion; epileptic diagnosis requires different supporting evidence.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071

questions.question: During appropriately monitored carotid sinus massage in a 72-year-old with unexplained falls, a 4-second pause occurs but no spontaneous-type symptom is reproduced. What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity; carotid sinus syndrome is not established by the pause alone
Definite carotid sinus syndrome requiring pacing regardless of symptom correlation
A normal response because asystole is less than six seconds
Proof of intrinsic sinus node disease
questions.explanation:
Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity Versus Syndrome

Correct answer: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity; carotid sinus syndrome is not established by the pause alone

Diagnostic Distinction

**Hypersensitivity:** ventricular pause >3 seconds and/or SBP fall ==>50 mmHg== during massage.

Carotid sinus syndrome requires compatible spontaneous events reproduced by the test; symptom-producing pauses are often longer.

Safe Testing

**Use ECG and beat-to-beat BP monitoring** in an appropriate clinical setting, usually age >40 with a compatible unexplained reflex presentation.

**Assess cerebrovascular/carotid contraindications first.**

Recent stroke/TIA or significant carotid stenosis requires avoidance or specialist risk assessment; the test is not an unmonitored bedside experiment.

Definite carotid sinus syndrome requiring pacing regardless of symptom correlation: Asymptomatic hypersensitivity is common in older people; syndrome diagnosis requires reproduction of compatible spontaneous symptoms and clinical correlation.

A normal response because asystole is less than six seconds: A pause exceeding three seconds meets the conventional hypersensitivity criterion; absence of symptoms limits the syndrome inference rather than making the response normal.

Proof of intrinsic sinus node disease: A provoked reflex pause does not by itself establish intrinsic sinus-node failure; mechanism and spontaneous rhythm evidence must be distinguished.

ESC Syncope Guideline, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy037

ESC Practical Instructions for Syncope, 2018 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehy071
